Question: Was Eva Longoria's Flamin' Hot Cheetos movie fact, fiction, or both?
Answer: It depends on who you talk to, whether the movie was fact, fiction, or both. The June 13, 2023, Los Angeles Times column by Gustavo Arellano was titled: “Why the Flamin’ Hot Cheetos movie is both pandering and pernicious.” Those were pretty strong “P-words,” but Arellano called it as he saw it. Of course, Eva Longoria was less than thrilled with the article. The movie was her directorial debut, and she was very proud of the film. A scene from “Flamin’ Hot,” a film directed by Eva Longoria about the purported origins of Flamin’ Hot Cheetos. (Searchlight Pictures) The Perfect Journalist To Write The “Flamin’ Hot” Article - Ask A Mexican Gustavo Arellano was the perfect journalist to review the film with a unique perspective on the Mexican American community. Arellano is a highly respected American writer and featured contributor for the Los Angeles Times. He is also the former publisher and editor of Orange County’s alternative paper, OC Weekly. He is also an integral part of the Latino community. Ask A Mexican He is most notably the author of the column jAsk a Mexican! Which is syndicated nationally and has been collected into book form as ¡Ask a Mexican! (Scribner, 2008). Arellano is highly respected as a journalist. Arellano has won numerous awards for the ¡Ask a Mexican! Column, including the 2006 and 2008 Best Non-Political Column in a large-circulation weekly from the Association of Alternative Newsweeklies. He was also awarded the impressive 2007 Presidents Award from the Los Angeles Press Club, an Impacto Award from the National Hispanic Media Coalition, and a 2008 Latino Spirit award from the California Latino Legislative Caucus. The man knows the Latino community and writes from a position of honor and authority. If he describes Longoria’s movie as “pandering and pernicious,” it’s noteworthy. Liar Liar Pants On Fire? Did real-life-janitor-turned-Frito-Lay-executive Richard Montañez really invent Flamin’ Hot Cheetos? Or was he spinning a fairy tale? In 2021 Los Angeles Times writer Sam Dean published an article proving that Montañez was a fibber at best and a fabulist at worst. Hot Cheetos lovers accused the Los Angeles Times of trying to takedown Montañez. But Deam was reporting the facts. Eva Longoria Was Not Happy With The Los Angeles Times Eva Longoria was interviewed by the Los Angeles Times in the spring of 2023 before the movie was released. She dismissed Dean’s reporting by snickering: “[It] feels like L.A. Times would have better resources dedicated to more important things.” For decades, the National Hispanic Media Coalition has righteously called out anti-Latino bias in Hollywood and the national media. They responded to the Montañez criticism from the media by releasing a news release urging people to see “Flamin’ Hot.” L.A. Plaza de Cultura y Artes in downtown Los Angeles hosted a packed outdoor screening earlier in June attended by Longoria, Montañez, and Dolores Huerta (one of the most influential labor activists of the 20th century). The goal was to support Longoria’s film. A Charming Feel-Good Movie Whether It’s A Fairy Tale Or Not I completely believed Dean's findings, but I'm a long-time Eva Longoria fan. I watched "Flamin' Hot." I found it charming and inspirational. Even though I knew about the film’s truth-telling controversy. Besides my appreciation of Longoria, I would have watched the filn just to see Tony Shalhoub (Monk) as Frito-Lay's CEO, Roger Enrico. I also love Dennis Haysber (Clarence C. Baker). He;s also one of my favorites. Should The Facts Be Damned? Yes, I understand the ethical concerns Sam Dean, Gustavo Arellano, and The Los Angeles Times raised. Monica Castillo also raised similar concerns in her June 9, 2023, review of “Flamin’ Hot” for RogerEbertcom. Castillo wrote: “Do we, as a woefully underrepresented group in movies, need this story, facts be damned? As a Latina critic who has been writing about my community’s stories for as long as I’ve had a career, I want better for us and our storytellers. While I enjoy some aspects of this movie, I’m not sure the means justified the lackluster result. Instead, Longoria's film becomes an extended lesson in tying a product to cultural identity, targeting an audience, and how to monetize them as prospective consumers. It’s just business, baby, and sometimes the characters in the middle get lost in the capitalist shuffle. Then again, Montañez’s self-mythologizing is his business, and this movie is now an extension of those efforts to rewrite history—a product placement, if you will—cinematically solidifying his alleged role in a product he didn’t create.” Longoria Is A Staunch Supporter Of The Latina Community Castillo noted: “My ethical qualms aside, Longoria channels the hard-working Mexican American/Latino/immigrant ethos in her film, showing genuine love and respect for the hustle that keeps food on the table and the lights on despite impossible odds,” “What does it say when we lionize a person who says they did something they didn’t and hold them up as a pillar of our community, who, if anything, perfected selling our connections to our culture back to ourselves as a form of identity consumerism?” Indeed, what does it say? All very good points. Artistic License Can Be Fraught With Danger As a writer, I understand the desire to punch up a story to add drama or entertainment. But I also worry about wandering too far from the truth. I recently finished my first true crime book for publication and worried incessantly about getting the facts right. I nagged my editors to avoid introducing any word art that might stretch artistic license. I understand the dilemma Longoria and her writers might have struggled to overcome. Their are many fine lines. The Life Of Richard Montañez Is Inspirational What is true about the film is that Montañez’s life is an inspiration. He really was a high school dropout from Ontario who rose through the ranks of Frito-Lay and now travels the country to speak about his unlikely rise. But as Sam Dean pointed out in his 2021 LA Times article, Montañez didn’t invent Flamin’ Hot Cheetos — others at Frito-Lay did. The film states that Montañez came up with the idea for Hot Cheetos in 1992, even though Dean’s article showed that was the year the snack debuted nationwide after ongoing successful test runs in Texas and the Midwest. Credit should always be given to those who truly deserve it. As Gustavo Arellano summarizes: “The details of history don’t matter to Longoria; Mexican pride does. “Flamin’ Hot” is the type of feel-good treacle that high school teachers screened for their Mexican American students when I was coming of age in the 1990s to make us feel better about ourselves. Teachers today will no doubt do the same for their students. That’s what makes “Flamin Hot” not just pandering but pernicious.” The Takeaway Although I enjoyed the film, I knew before I watched it that Richard Montañez did not personally invent Flamin' Hot Cheetos. I give Longoria kudos for her work and directorial debut, which must be deemed successful on many levels. Not everyone will love the film, but I found it charming. Kudos need to go to Gustavo Arellano, Sam Dean, and Monica Castillo for honoring journalistic integrity and reporting the true facts about Richard Montañez. In the world of 2023, it's comforting to know that there are still writers willing to risk criticism by speaking their truth. Thank you to Arellano, Dean, and Castillo. Should you see the film? It's a good story about a young man who beat the odds to build a great life for his family. Is Eva Longoria's Flamin' Hot Cheetos movie fact, fiction, or both? It’s both. Just remember the story has some elements of fantasy. Then sit back and be entertained.

Question: How has Bruce Willis' family supported him during his health struggles?
Answer: Bruce Willis’ family is doing whatever they can to support him with his aphasia diagnosis. A source said the actor’s wife, ex-wife, and five children have all “rallied around him in a big way.” Willis’s family announced via a coordinated social media post in 2022 that Willis “has been experiencing some health issues and has recently been diagnosed with aphasia, which is impacting his cognitive abilities.” Bruce Willis - Wikipedia Due to the diagnosis, the actor, 68, decided to step away “from the career that has meant so much to him.” His wife, Emma Heming Willis, their two young daughters, Mabel and Evelyn, his ex-wife Demi Moore, and their three adult daughters, Rumer, Scout, and Tallulah, all signed the Social Media message, explaining, “This is a really challenging time for our family, and we appreciate your continued love, compassion, and support. We are moving through this as a strong family unit and wanted to bring his fans in because we know how much he means to you, as you do to him. As Bruce always says, ‘Live it up,’ and we plan to do just that together.” An insider said the family is trying to treasure their time with Willis. “Emma is especially grateful for the daughters she shares with Bruce,” “Everyone is focused on all the happy moments they can share,” they added. Another source close to the actor explained that his family is focused on “doing whatever they can [to support him],” and “They have rallied around him in a big way to help Bruce cope with what is to come.” While a source close to Emma concluded, “As someone facing health challenges, Bruce couldn’t be part of a better family. It’s been shocking. And it’s not easy seeing a spouse decline. But she’s trying to keep it together for him.” Tallulah Willis Shared In Vogue Magazine How She Is Dealing With Her Dad Tallulah Willis, the youngest daughter of Bruce and Demi Moore, recently wrote an essay that was published in Vogue Magazine. She shared her own struggles with her eating disorder and her diagnosis of Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD). “She talked about what she is doing with regard. to dealing with her dad: "I can bring him an energy that's bright and sunny, no matter where I've been. In the past, I was so afraid of being destroyed by sadness, but finally, I feel I can show up and be relied upon. I can savor that time, hold my dad's hand and feel that it's wonderful. I know that trials are looming, that this is the beginning of grief, but that whole thing about loving yourself before you can love somebody else — it's real." Tallulah said she documents every hangout with her dad, whose mobility has not been impacted by FTD. "Recently, I found a scrap of paper there on which he had written, simply, 'Michael Jordan.' I wish I knew what he was thinking. (In any case, I took it!)," she shared. "He still knows who I am and lights up when I enter the room. (He may always know who I am, give or take the occasional bad day. One difference between frontotemporal dementia (FTD)FTD) and Alzheimer's dementia is that, at least early in the disease, the former is characterized by language and motor deficits, while the latter features more memory loss.) I keep flipping between the present and the past when I talk about Bruce: he is, he was, he is, he was. That's because I have hopes for my father that I'm so reluctant to let go of," Tallulah added. Meanwhile, the entire family is doing their best to cherish every minute with him that they can. Best wishes to all.

Question: Who is Robert Kennedy Jr. married to?
Answer: As of July 2023, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is still legally married to actress Cheryl Hines. The actress and Robert F. Kennedy Jr got married in 2014. Known by his initials RFK Jr., he offered to announce that he had separated from Cheryl Hines to shield her from the scrutiny of his political statements. Cheryl Hines - Wikipedia In a new interview with the New York Times, Hines’ first since Kennedy announced his candidacy in the 2024 presidential run, the actor reiterates that she supports her husband’s political aspirations and understands her growing role in the campaign — noting how her public persona “feels different because it feels like every word is important” and that “people are listening in a different way.” Hines shares that the statement that drove Kennedy to propose the separation announcement was his comparisons between the Holocaust and CDC leader Anthony Fauci’s efforts to vaccinate Americans against COVID. Hines will not agree to a separation for political reasons. She said: “I support Bobby, and I want to be there for him, and I want him to feel loved and supported by me,” reiterates Hines.
